rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods / Results - the study reports its own laboratory anticlogging tests (10 weekly cycles, two laterals systems with and without 2% urea), urea adsorption kinetics, microbial counts, XRD/FE-SEM of clogging materials and discharge reduction rate (Fig. 4, Fig. 5, Table 4, Table 5).
rows.notes: The study is a laboratory emitter-clogging experiment with muddy water and urea fertigation; no crops were grown and no yield, crop quality or nutrient-uptake outcomes were measured. It cannot support the claim that automated/advanced drip irrigation increases crop yield, optimises quality or reduces excessive nutrient consumption versus conventional drip. The study actually shows that 2% urea in muddy water changes clogging materials (calcite, actinomycetes), inhibits bacteria/fungi, and after ~35 days increases the discharge reduction rate relative to muddy water without urea. The technology compared (urea fertigation vs no urea, same emitters) is not an ADI-vs-conventional-DIS comparison.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods / Results - own laboratory anticlogging experiment with measured emitter discharge, dry weight of clogging materials, microbial counts and mineral composition (Figs. 2-5, Tables 4-5).
rows.notes: No pesticide application or pest/disease outcome was measured or discussed; the study concerns emitter clogging under urea muddy-water fertigation. The only biological measurements are counts of bacteria, fungi and actinomycetes in lateral sediments as clogging agents, which is unrelated to pesticide reduction in crops. The technology (urea fertigation through standard inline emitters) is also not ADI versus conventional DIS.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). The review citations (Liu et al., 2019a/2019b) attribute to this study effects on water/fertilizer saving, yield, quality and pesticide reduction that it does not test; it is a bench-scale emitter clogging study with no crop.
